clue.text: 'Don't get so excited'? I'm astonished and illuminated!

blocks.note: an exclamation of surprise, as in 'Coo, look at that!'
lit up, given light

explanation.surface: Someone startled and dazzled is told to calm down by a companion.
explanation.walkthrough: COO is a dated British cry of amazement; the two halves read like a reply to the calming advice.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is an idiomatic instruction to calm down, stay relaxed and stop getting worked up.

clue.text: Sweet treat, cold, with superior casing

indicators.note: a casing wraps around what it holds, so the word for superior is placed outside

blocks.note: C is the abbreviation for cold, as on a tap
choice as an adjective means of top quality

explanation.surface: A dessert is described as chilled and wrapped in a classy shell.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads like a description of the dessert itself, but it is wordplay. A choc ice is a British freezer staple: ice cream coated in chocolate.
explanation.definitionFit: This British confection is a bar of ice cream with a chocolate coating, a frozen dessert treat.

clue.text: Toothsome Ganymede, essentially Greek character

indicators.note: essentially points to the core of the phrase, the letters sitting inside its words

blocks.note: the letters run across the join of the two words

explanation.surface: Ganymede, the beautiful youth of Greek myth, is praised as a tasty figure.
explanation.definitionFit: It is the last letter of the Greek alphabet, and a letter is a character in writing.

clue.text: One of us overheard where vitamin C can be found

indicators.note: something overheard is caught by ear, so the phrase is judged by its sound

blocks.clueFragment: where vitamin C can be found
blocks.note: cider is made from apples, which contain vitamin C

explanation.surface: A member of the group lets slip a nutritional fact.
explanation.walkthrough: The location phrase 'in cider' is said the same as the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone within a group or organisation, rather than an outsider, counts as one of us.

clue.text: Break-fast time?

blocks.note: surface reading: the hour for the morning meal
setter's reading: the moment a long religious fast is broken, at the end of Lent

explanation.surface: Someone asks when the morning meal is served.
explanation.walkthrough: The hyphen splits breakfast into 'break fast': Christians fast through Lent and end it at this festival.
explanation.definitionFit: The Christian festival marks the end of the forty days of Lent, when fasting is traditionally broken.

clue.text: 19 martial arts are on the rise? Not entirely

indicators.note: not entirely means only part of the phrase is used, a run inside it
in a down clue, rising means reading from the bottom upward, so backwards

blocks.note: a run of letters across the end of the first word and the next two

explanation.surface: A puzzle reference suggests martial arts are growing in popularity, with a hedge.
explanation.walkthrough: 19 refers to 19-down, STELLAR, which serves as the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Astral and stellar both mean relating to the stars, so the adjectives are synonyms.

clue.text: Company, they say, with problem, so it's said: Freeman Hardy Willis, say

indicators.note: so it's said tells us the preceding word counts by how it is pronounced

blocks.note: from the saying 'three's company'
a sum is an arithmetic problem

explanation.surface: A shoe-shop chain's name is discussed amid talk of firms and difficulties.
explanation.walkthrough: Freeman, Hardy and Willis was a British shoe chain named after three people, so it is an example of a trio.
explanation.definitionFit: The chain's name joins three surnames, making it a group of three, an example of the answer.

clue.text: Twig taken from trees all Gipsies regularly ignored

indicators.note: skipping letters at regular intervals leaves every other one

blocks.note: the even-placed letters, starting with the second

explanation.surface: A small branch is cut from trees while the travellers look away.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Twig' looks like a branch, but here it is the informal verb meaning to catch on.
explanation.definitionFit: In British slang to twig is to understand or catch on, the same as becoming aware of something.

clue.text: Rhyme, but not reason?

blocks.note: surface reading: the idiom 'neither rhyme nor reason', meaning no sense at all
setter's reading: poetry that rhymes yet makes no sense, like Lear's limericks

explanation.surface: A twist on the phrase 'without rhyme or reason'.
explanation.definitionFit: Edward Lear and Lewis Carroll wrote comic, rhyming poems that deliberately make no sense.

clue.text: DCI endlessly wedded to poetical writing: Morse is a good example

indicators.note: without ends means both outside letters are dropped, leaving only the centre

blocks.note: the abbreviation for Detective Chief Inspector
a lyric poem

explanation.surface: Detective Chief Inspector Morse is wedded to poetry, as the TV character was.
explanation.walkthrough: Inspector Morse is the fictional Oxford detective, but the definition wants Morse's dots-and-dashes system.
explanation.definitionFit: Morse is a signalling system turning letters into dots and dashes, a classic example of encoding.

clue.text: Insufficient funds to obtain biscuits

blocks.note: lacking enough
slang for money

explanation.surface: Someone is too broke to buy a packet of biscuits.
explanation.definitionFit: The Scottish buttery confection is a rich crumbly biscuit, often baked in fingers or rounds.

clue.text: Disrespectfully, the Queen's on the side of a road leading to a windswept village

blocks.note: an over-familiar short name for Queen Elizabeth
taken as written
the abbreviation for road

explanation.surface: The monarch stands on a roadside on the way to a blustery hamlet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On the side of' just places the name beside the next pieces. Lizard is a village in Cornwall near Lizard Point, Britain's most southerly mainland tip.
explanation.definitionFit: The Cornish settlement sits on an exposed peninsula at Britain's southernmost point, battered by sea gales.

clue.text: Miracle cure: get practically starkers, caked in dirt

indicators.note: practically means almost, so the word falls just short of complete
something caked in mud is wrapped by it, so one piece sits within the other

blocks.note: starkers is British slang for naked; drop the final letter
earth or muck

explanation.surface: A quack's advice: strip off and roll in mud for a miracle cure.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase names a fraudulent remedy sold by quacks as a cure for everything.

clue.text: Spicy snacks go with Italian lager

blocks.note: energy, as in 'full of go'
a well-known Italian beer brand

explanation.surface: Spicy nibbles are paired with a cold Italian beer.
explanation.definitionFit: This spicy Italian-American salami is eaten in slices as a snack or on pizza.

clue.text: One who you hope leaves their coat in your home

definitions.text: One who you hope leaves their coat in your home

blocks.clueFragment: One who you hope leaves their coat in your home
blocks.note: surface reading: a forgetful guest whose jacket you'd keep
setter's reading: a layer of finish applied to the walls

explanation.surface: A host oddly wishes a visitor would forget their jacket.
explanation.walkthrough: Coat means a layer of material spread on a wall, not a garment.
explanation.definitionFit: The tradesperson spreads a smooth layer of lime or gypsum over interior walls and ceilings.

clue.text: Goitre has no appeal: it's a queasy sight

indicators.note: having none of something means it is taken out of the word

blocks.note: a swelling of the thyroid gland
sex appeal, as in 'she's got it'

explanation.surface: A swollen neck is unattractive and makes people feel queasy.
explanation.definitionFit: Spilt blood and violence in films can turn the stomach, making it a nauseating spectacle.

clue.text: Scammers, pests and menaces, primarily

indicators.note: primarily means in the first place, so the leading letter of each word

blocks.note: the initials of the four words

explanation.surface: A list of the nuisances behind unwanted messages.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue also describes the answer: junk email comes from scammers and pests.
explanation.definitionFit: Unsolicited bulk email is sent by fraudsters and nuisances, so the clue describes it entirely.

clue.text: Embarrassing when ghastly performer appears in chorus

indicators.note: to appear in something is to be inside it, so one piece goes within the other

blocks.note: a ham is an overacting, bad actor
to sing together, as a chorus does

explanation.surface: It's mortifying when a dreadful turn turns up in the backing singers.
explanation.definitionFit: Shaming and embarrassing both describe causing someone humiliation, so the adjectives are synonyms.

clue.text: I'd like to sleep easy after a massage

indicators.note: a massage kneads and reshapes, so the letters are worked into new order

blocks.note: the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone hopes for a good night's rest after a relaxing rub-down.
explanation.definitionFit: Accepting an offer politely, the reply means 'I would welcome that', the same as 'I'd like that'.

clue.text: Sauce added principally into Italian food?

definitions.text: Sauce added principally into Italian food?

indicators.note: principally means first of all, so the opening letters of the two words
putting something into a dish places it inside it

blocks.note: the initials of the two words
Italy's staple of noodles and shapes

explanation.surface: A cook asks if this is the sauce stirred into an Italian dish.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue also defines the answer: a tomato sauce mostly added to pasta.
explanation.definitionFit: Passata is sieved uncooked tomato purée, commonly used as the base sauce for Italian pasta dishes.

clue.text: Sell, rat out: characteristic of The Sun, etc

indicators.note: out suggests disorder or being put wrong, so the letters are scrambled

blocks.note: the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A tabloid informant is told to betray someone and sell the story to The Sun.
explanation.walkthrough: The Sun is a British tabloid newspaper, but here it is the star at the centre of our solar system.
explanation.definitionFit: The Sun is a star, so anything characteristic of it and other stars is of the stars.

clue.text: Quietly pounce and land in water

blocks.note: p, piano, is the musical marking for soft
a sudden forward spring

explanation.surface: A predator creeps up, springs and ends up in a pond.
explanation.definitionFit: A plunge is a dive or sudden drop into water, ending up submerged after jumping.

clue.text: French can add butter to both sides of 'pain'

indicators.note: something on both sides of another piece surrounds it

blocks.note: to baste is to moisten food with fat while it cooks
an ill is a trouble or harm

explanation.surface: A French cook butters both sides of the bread, 'pain' being French for bread.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pain' looks like the French word for bread, but it is read in English. 'Can' is slang for prison.
explanation.definitionFit: The Bastille was the notorious Paris prison stormed in 1789, and 'can' is slang for a jail.

clue.text: 'Vigorously resist habits' - one who has them

indicators.note: doing something vigorously shakes it up, so the letters are thrown around

blocks.note: the letters to be rearranged
surface padding: the thing the definition's 'them' points back to

explanation.surface: A slogan urging people to fight bad habits, credited to someone who has them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Habits' looks like bad tendencies; the definition reads it as the nun's robes.
explanation.definitionFit: A nun is addressed as Sister, and nuns wear the long robes called habits.

clue.text: At the outset, straining posterior muscle produces an amusing noise

indicators.note: the outset is the start, so only each word's opening letter is used

blocks.note: the opening letters of these two words
short for latissimus dorsi, a large back muscle

explanation.surface: Straining your backside muscles makes a comic sound.
explanation.definitionFit: Splat is the comic sound of something soft and wet hitting a surface, the stuff of cartoons.

clue.text: With time to spare, foolishly romanticise a far-off place

indicators.note: time to spare is time left over and set aside, so it is taken out
acting foolishly is acting in a muddled way, so the letters are jumbled

blocks.note: the abbreviation for time
the word to have its letters rearranged

explanation.surface: With idle hours, someone daydreams about an exotic distant destination.
explanation.definitionFit: This Pacific island region lies thousands of miles from Britain, making it a remote destination.

clue.text: White lie, mostly tall story ultimately

indicators.note: mostly means not all, so the final letter is dropped
ultimately means in the end, so only the closing letter of each word is kept

blocks.note: a falsehood
the final letter of each of the two words

explanation.surface: A harmless fib turns out, in the end, to be a tall tale.
explanation.walkthrough: 'White lie' reads as one phrase, but 'White' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Lily is used as an adjective for pure white, as in lily-white hands or skin.

clue.text: The aged are welcomed into German band

indicators.note: being welcomed into a place means going inside it

blocks.note: the old form, as in 'thou art'
the abbreviation for German

explanation.surface: Elderly people are welcomed into a German group of musicians.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The aged are' means 'are' as old English said it. 'Band' is a strip of material, not musicians.
explanation.definitionFit: A garter is an elastic strip worn round the leg to hold up a stocking.

clue.text: Rail is missing from banister

indicators.note: missing from the word means absent, so those letters are taken out

blocks.note: taken as written
a staircase handrail

explanation.surface: A handrail has lost part of its structure.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rail' and 'banister' look like the same staircase handrail; here 'Rail' is the verb to scold or mock.
explanation.definitionFit: To rail at someone is to jeer or tease them, close to the verb meaning to exchange teasing remarks.
